summary.text: Stellar nucleosynthesis is the creation of chemical elements by nuclear reactions within stars.
It explains why the observed abundances of elements change over time and why some elements and isotopes are much more abundant than others.
It has gone on since the Big Bang first made hydrogen, helium and lithium, and Fred Hoyle first proposed the theory in 1946.

facts.label: Proposed by
facts.value: Fred Hoyle in 1946, refined by him in 1954

facts.label: The B²FH paper
facts.value: A 1957 paper that became one of astrophysics' most cited

facts.label: Final burning
facts.value: A shock wave briefly raises temperatures by roughly 50%

facts.label: Hydrogen fusers
facts.value: Ninety percent of stars, except white dwarfs, fuse hydrogen

facts.label: Proton–proton yield
facts.value: About 26.2 MeV released per complete cycle

items.prompt: A star spends its life making heavier elements in its core. Why does that alone not much change the mix of elements in the universe?

options.label: The heavier elements break apart again at once
Stars make too little of any heavy element
Heavy elements cannot form inside any star
The new elements stay contained within the star

items.explain: The elements stay inside the star, so burning alone does not significantly alter universe-wide abundances; the star must eject material, as a planetary nebula or supernova.

items.prompt: Late in life, a low-mass star and a much higher-mass star both return material to space. How do the two differ?

options.label: The low-mass star explodes while the high-mass one fades quietly
The low-mass star sheds its atmosphere slowly; the high-mass star ejects mass in a sudden blast
Both explode in exactly the same way
Neither returns any material to space

items.explain: A low-mass star slowly ejects its atmosphere by stellar wind, forming a planetary nebula, while a higher-mass star ejects mass in a sudden supernova.

items.prompt: The core of a Sun-like star warms by 10%. What happens to the energy made by its dominant fusion process?

options.label: It rises by about 46%
It rises by about 10%
It stays about the same
It drops by about 10%

items.explain: The proton–proton chain depends on roughly T⁴, the fourth power of temperature, so a 10% rise increases its energy production by 46%.

items.prompt: Which hydrogen-fusing process becomes more important in a main-sequence star much more massive than the Sun?

options.label: The proton–proton chain
Fusion of silicon into nickel
The carbon–nitrogen–oxygen cycle
Chemical burning of hydrogen

items.explain: The proton–proton chain dominates up to about the Sun's mass, while the CNO cycle is more important in more massive main-sequence stars.

items.prompt: Plotted against atomic number, the Solar System's element abundances form a jagged sawtooth varying by factors of tens of millions. What did that hint at?

options.label: The elements were handed out at random
Every element is equally easy to make
A natural process that is not random
Only a few elements exist in the Solar System

items.explain: The jagged pattern suggested a natural process that is not random, which spurred the theory of nucleosynthesis.

items.prompt: Bethe's 1939 work explained how stars stay hot. What question did it leave open?

options.label: How stars find enough hydrogen to burn
How stars can shine for billions of years
How stars end up with a core at all
How heavier nuclei get created

items.explain: Bethe's papers concerned energy generation and did not address the creation of heavier nuclei; Hoyle began that theory in 1946.
